While I am on my feet, I should like to say, with regard to the question
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
that was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Pommer) having to do with Selkirk wheat, that there are only 3 million bushels of Selkirk wheat in western Canada. It takes about 40 million bushels to seed the crop, and about half of the area that has to be seeded will be in a district that was last year infected with rust, so that it would take in the neighbourhood of 20 million bushels to seed the area that was rusted. The government this year has therefore decided-and the action was taken by the wheat board-that they would not permit the export of this wheat, other than some 20,000 bushels which, I think, was supplied to the United States government. Any wheat which would be allowed to go out of Canada in future would result from dealings with the United States government.
The question asked yesterday was as to whether we would permit the boundary to be opened so that Selkirk wheat could move now. I understand that the reason for the question is that most of those in the southern part of Manitoba near the boundary line have disposed of all the Selkirk wheat they find it possible to dispose of, and they have some in surplus. My understanding is that the Saskatchewan government has been paying the freight on Selkirk wheat. They have at least been giving considerable assistance in the movement of Selkirk wheat from where it happened to be to where it was needed. With the price which is being obtained from these quantities, which are not necessarily certified grades, the price is such that farmers can buy the wheat, and it is being bought in Canada. My suggestion to those who live in parts of Manitoba that have already been supplied as far as possible is that they get in touch with the authorities in Saskatchewan or with the provincial government in Manitoba and find where that wheat can be marketed. It is not our desire that it be allowed to go out of Canada, except to the extent that it is being helpful to some activities of the government of the United States. We hope that it will be seeded in western Canada.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, April 25, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Marler-Mr. Robinson (Sim-coe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to consolidate the various enactments relating to Canadian National Railways into one statute, also, to provide that the Canadian National Railway Company may operate a telecommunication system, to authorize officers and employees of the Canadian National Railways to act as directors of partially-owned companies, to authorize the company to construct short lines without specific parliamentary authority and to operate motor vehicles and further to make provisions for extinguishing charters of constituent corporations.

Mr. Chairman, before the house rose at ten o'clock last evening I had a few words to say about the employment situation on the Canadian National Railways. I wish to express once again the earnest hope that at this time, when all the statutes repenting the Canadian National Railways are being reviewed, consolidated! and re-enacted, serious consideration will be given to the position of those who work for this railway.
As hon. members in all parts of the house are aware, there is considerable concern on the part of many members at the lay-offs that have been taking place. Our concern is
316G	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways nothing compared with the concern of the men themselves. Many of us feel that this government-owned railway, and the government behind it, owe to these men who work for the railway something better than the uncertainty and insecurity that they have been facing in recent weeks, and the uncertainty and insecurity that hangs over them so far as the future is concerned. Other matters in connection with the operations of the railway are important. Capital structure is a subject to which we must give attention. The acquiring of the best possible equipment is important. The maintenance of the equipment is important. But it is also important, indeed more important, that consideration be given to the position of the men. Out of the discussions on this legislation I hope may come the formulation of a policy that will put an end to the lay-offs that have been taking place and will provide some protection for these people who carry the main burden of the load so far as the operation of the Canadian National Railways is concerned.
As hon. members know, figures have been placed on the record this session. We also know that notices have been given of still further lay-offs at Winnipeg, Leaside, Toronto and other places. This is an extremely important matter. As strongly as I can I urge that there be the formulation of a policy that will remove this insecurity and uncertainty with regard to the employment of Canadian National workers.
It also seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that at a time when Canadian National Railways policies are being reviewed in their entirety, some attention should be paid to the position of retired C.N.R. employees.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Order. May I at this moment express a doubt that we are reviewing Canadian National Railways policy in its entirety. It seems to me that this resolution refers to a measure to consolidate into one statute the various enactments relating to the Canadian National Railways. It seems to me that it is merely a consolidation and, in my opinion, it would not give hon. members the privilege of discussing Canadian National Railways policy in general. The resolution goes on to mention certain particular matters which are the subject of amendment. It seems to me that this debate might be more properly directed, first of all, to a discussion of the advisability or inadvisability of consolidating the statutes and, second, to the various particular matters which are mentioned in the resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
If Your Honour is suggesting that discussion of detailed matters of policy should wait until we have the bill before us, I would not go out of my way to quarrel with you. But, sir, if you are suggesting that because all that is proposed is a consolidation of certain acts that are on the statute books we cannot discuss what is involved in the statutes that are being consolidated, I submit that I would have the right to take issue with you.
As Your Honour is aware, the deputy chairman of committees of the whole raised this point at ten o'clock last evening. Since then I have taken the trouble to do a little bit of homework on the point and, if I may say so, with respect, I think some confusion arises because there are citations in May, particularly in May as revised by Campion, which suggest that consolidating acts are dealt with expeditiously and without discussion of the details of the various acts being consolidated. I would point out, however, that that is because in the United Kingdom-unlike here in Canada-there is what is known as the consolidation of enactments (procedure) act, 1949, under which it is possible for statutes of the parliament of the United Kingdom to be consolidated in what is referred to in May as an expeditious manner. I therefore suggest that the citations in May which limit discussion of bills that consolidate do not apply to this parliament because we have no such measure. We have no provision that puts consolidating acts in any other category than that of any bill that comes before parliament.
All I am saying is this. If you agree with me I will leave the matter until a later date. If you feel that this discussion should wait until we have the bill before us and if it is understood that when the bill is before us we can discuss on the bill any of the matters referred to in the bill, I have no objection to waiting until that occasion. But if there is any suggestion that we cannot discuss what is in that bill, perhaps that will be a point for further discussion when the time comes. I wonder whether Your Honour could indicate whether it is your view merely that this discussion should wait until the bill is before us or whether it is your view that these matters should not be discussed at all.

Hon. members will know that in our practice, on discussion of the bill, it is the principle of the amending bill, not the principle of the bill which it is proposed to amend, which we are allowed to discuss. One might say that the same consideration might be applicable to discussion of the resolution which precedes the bill.
(Mr. Knowles.]

Hon. members will recall that standing order 58, subparagraph 2, reads as follows:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
This is an interesting and rather important point. In one light, it might be considered that an amending bill which merely consolidates various enactments which now appear in different acts is nothing more or less than a renumbering of certain sections. I do not think that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would argue that if an enactment were being amended by the insertion of a new clause and the later clauses were being renumbered, he would have the privilege of debating the principles of all those later clauses.
I should like to give the matter further consideration before making a definite ruling. As I said, the point is important, interesting and probably rather new. But in one light, I do not believe that a mere consolidation statute opens up the entire original acts for discussion at this stage. As I say, I would not wish to rule too definitely on the point without giving the matter mature consideration, but at the moment my feeling is that a consolidation is little more than a renumbering. It would be difficult to see how a consolidation should properly open up the entire act to discussion, bearing in mind the well-known principle which I first stated, namely, that it is the principle of the amending bill which is discussed. The hon. member will of course realize that there are other and perhaps better opportunities to discuss the subjects which he has indicated he might wish to discuss at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I was most interested in what you said a minute ago about the discussion that should take place on a resolution preceding a bill. May I respectfully suggest that the resolution is the cornerstone of the bill itself. Originally such a resolution was introduced before the bill was drafted in order to give all members an opportunity to make suggestions for the better drafting of the bill. This is why I find discussion of the resolution so important. I do not know whether or not the bill has been drafted but valuable and constructive suggestions could be made by members and listened to by the minister and the government, as the result of which the tenor of the bill could be entirely different from what it would be if such a discussion had not taken place.
Whether the bill is a condensation, compilation or totally new legislation makes practically no difference because constructive suggestions in the house shall always be welcomed by the government as well as by the whole membership of the house. In the first place, hon. members know that at Westminster there are not enough seats for all members of the House of Commons and therefore members very often speak in turn. Some speak on the resolution preceding a bill, others on second reading, others on the bill in committee, and others on third reading of the bill. This is one of the reasons why the numerous readings are so important and cannot be dispensed with.
Naturally this is an opinion I am offering. The other day I was called an expert on procedure, which I deny completely. I have never claimed to be an expert on parliamentary procedure. I have been here for 31 years, and for 29 years I have had the opportunity to express my views freely in the house. But in my humble view experts in parliamentary procedure are dangerous people who make procedure difficult to understand in order to pose as the only ones who know anything about it. It is a very dangerous mentality. I speak as a member of parliament who has been here for a great number of years and who has done his best to establish a relation between what he had to say and what was before the house. That
3168	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways is one of my understandings of the few main rules that relate to discussion in the house.
Turning to the resolution now before us, it is one of the most important that has come before us this year. It is no less than a compilation of all the laws that concern the Canadian National Railways. There was so much legislation about the Canadian National Railways that some of the statutes we find in the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1952 are still separate one from the other. As a preamble to what I am going to say, I should like to remind you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee of what has happened with regard to the Canadian National Railways. First of all we had the Intercolonial which was managed by the minister of railways and canals himself. He had full authority with regard to the railway. Then there were some new railways that were built and which were bought by the Canadian government. During the first world war the Grand Trunk was purchased. Then the Canadian Northern was purchased and Mr. Gutelius was put in charge not of the Intercolonial Railway but of the Canadian government railways which included the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern. There was a lot of misunderstanding between the employees of the old Intercolonial Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway.
Mr. Gutelius came from the United States to manage the Canadian government railways. Then he was succeeded by Mr. D. B. Hanna, a gentleman who had been with the Canadian Northern in the first place. He took charge of the Canadian government railways. It happened during the Borden-Meighen regime. As soon as the Liberals came to power in 1921 propaganda was started by the Conservative newspapers to the effect that the Canadian National Railways should be free to decide their own policies without any interference by the government. The idea behind that propaganda of the Conservative press was to prevent the Conservatives who were managing the railway from being replaced by Liberals. It was done for a political purpose, in order to maintain complete Tory control of the Canadian government railways. Then, Sir Henry Thornton came. He came with a good reputation because during the war he had been in the British Isles doing some excellent work in transportation. He was quite exacting. He wanted to be appointed chairman of the board of directors and president of the railway, two positions that are entirely different and cannot be associated together in a practical manner. The legislation was changed


and a new act was passed. Sir Henry Thornton became president of the railway and chairman of the board of directors.
According to the Canadian National Railways Act, chapter 40 of the Revised Statutes of 1952, the Canadian government railways or the former Intercolonial Railway, the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Northern system, formed the Canadian National Railways and the governor general in council may nominate not less than five nor more than seventeen persons to be directors of the Canadian National Railways. These directors shall be and are hereby incorporated as a company under the name of the Canadian National Railway Company, not the Canadian National Railways system, as Mr. Gordon stated before the committee the other day.
One should also draw attention to the fact that no stock ownership shall be necessary to qualify a director. The directors, therefore, represent not only the government of Canada but the people of Canada at large. They are there to fulfil a duty, which is a duty of control of the management of the railway.
Now, sir, the board of directors is entirely different from the management officers, with one exception which is that the chairman of the board of directors is also the president of the officers of the railway. The board of directors is as follows: Chairman, Mr. Donald Gordon, C.M.G., LL.D.; Mr. Wilfrid Gagnon, C.B.E.; Mr. J. A. Northey; Mr. H. J. Symington, C.M.G., Q.C.; Mr. R. B. Brenan; Mr. B. L. Daly; Mr. W. J. Parker. With regard to the officers, their names are mentioned in letters that are easier to read than those of the directors, and are contained on the first page of the last report of the Canadian National Railways. They are, Mr. Donald Gordon, C.M.G., LL.D, president; law, Mr. MacMillan, Q.C.; operating, Mr. S. F. Dingle, vice-president; the vice-president of the western region, Winnipeg; the vice-president of the central region, Toronto; the vice-president and general manager, Atlantic region, Moncton; the vice-president and general manager of the Grand Trunk Western Railroad, Detroit; the vice-president of personnel; the vice-president of purchasing and stores; the vice-president of research and development and the vice-president of traffic. There is a president and ten vicepresidents whose duties are entirely different from the board of directors.
I appreciate the good work that the Minister of Transport has done since he assumed that high office. His knowledge of the law makes him familiar with all the

intricacies of the management of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railways is a big company, a company with an income and expenditure, on the average, of $600 million a year. I have some sympathy for Mr. Gordon, and I expressed it to him before the committee. I said I thought he was working too hard. On March 31 last, Mr. Gordon said:
No man works harder; no man has more frustrations, and no man has more fun than I have.
This shows that he has a complex character, but a happy disposition. I quote the following from the committee report:
If you come here, it is in order to permit the members of parliament to help you, and we can do so only inasmuch as we know the facts.

Mr. Speaker, the debate at the resolution stage affords me an opportunity of acquainting the house and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) with a project calculated to promote the growth of the city of Alma, county seat of Lake St. John, and also to provide the Canadian National Railways with an additional source of revenue.
One of the clauses of the bill to be introduced following this resolution provides that the Canadian National Railways will be authorized to build short lines without specific parliamentary authority.
By virtue of these new powers, then, the Canadian National Railways could extend the present line from St. Gedeon to St. Joseph d'Alma, thence back to Hebertville Station to continue on to Jonquiere and Chicoutimi.
The route followed by this road was that of the first of our railway lines, constructed some 75 years ago to answer the needs of colonization. The parish of St. Joseph d'Alma had barely been established then, its population was only a few hundred and a small lumber industry had just been set up.
Since then, the Saguenay-Lake St. John district has expanded wonderfully. Lumber companies were first in their efforts to further the industrial growth of the Lake St. John district. At present it boasts six mills producing wood pulp and newsprint. Aluminum followed and gave its powerful impetus to the industrialization of what is commonly known as the Saguenay kingdom. The town of Alma, situated in the very heart of the Lake St. John district, has not in the least trailed behind other towns of the Saguenay
Canadian National Railways with respect to that development. What was a tiny village 75 years ago has become an industrial and commercial centre numbering nearly 15,000 people. It is the home town of most of the workers of the Riverbend mill, which produces nearly 700 tons of newsprint a day and employs 800 people. The aluminum smelter of Isle Maligne employs 1,200 workers who live in the towns of Isle Maligne, Naud-ville and Alma.
That community of close to 20,000 people is served by a modern hospital and a 1,000-watt radio station. Last year the Department of Transport recognized the importance of the town of Alma when it authorized the Boreal Airways Ltd., to use it as a stop-over on the Bagotville-Chibougamau flight, and has granted generous subsidies for the building of a municipal airport. Quite recently the Department of Public Works, realizing the fast growth of the chief town in the Lake St. John district, decided to put up a modern building to accommodate federal public services.
I am not asking the Canadian National management to "blaze the trail" or even to follow suit. All I am asking is that they recognize the rapid and steady development of that important industrial community which gives them more than a quarter of all the revenue from the Lake St. John line, with its outlets into Quebec and Montreal.
People who contribute such a substantial revenue to the Canadian National Railways should benefit from lower transportation rates and to have available within their district, or rather at their doorstep, a railway ensuring a fast and convenient passenger service.
Because the hon. Minister of Transport has never failed to give my requests his kind consideration, I hope that, when conferring upon the authorities of the Canadian National Railways the supplementary powers provided in the bill, he will ask the company to give top priority, among the short lines contemplated, to the extension of the railroad going from St. Gedeon to the town of Alma and thence to the station of Hebertville. The national railways will find it an additional source of revenue, while the population of the industrial centre formed by Alma, Naud-ville, Riverbend and Isle Maligne will be pleased to see that their long-cherished dream will at last come true.

If the hon. member will reread Hansard of February 7 he will find the opinion there given was that of Mr. J. R. McMillan, vice-president of the railway in Winnipeg, and not that of the Minister of Transport.
That sounds to me like a facetious play on words and not the kind of information to which the railway employees of this country are entitled. Let me go on. On February 28 last I had a motion before the house which was in the following terms:
For a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the minister or Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways relative to a question placed on the order paper in the name of the mover of this matter on the 28th January last, the purpose of which was to ascertain the number of section and maintenance men, office staffs, etc., who have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways during the periods particularly set forth in the said question.
You will remember what the answer was, Mr. Chairman. The answer was that such information was not procurable because the Canadian National Railways did not keep the kind of books that would give the information-and that on a railroad as large as the Canadian National. That aroused the employees everywhere throughout the country. If the railway does not have such records it is time they started to keep them. Certainly they spend enough money on staffs to be able to furnish that simple information.
On March 7, as found at page 1762 of Hansard, the following question was asked by the hon. member for Royal:
1.	How many hourly rated employees of the Canadian National Railways were laid off between January 1, 1954 and December 31, 1954?
2.	How many monthly rated employees "official capacity" of the Canadian National Railways were laid off between January 1, 1954 and December 31, 1954?

This was the answer by the minister:
The management of the Canadian National Railways advise that in order to answer the question as asked it would be necessary to secure information from divisional, district, regional and headquarters offices and require a special staff . . .
Then he went on to refer to the number of employees in the employ of Canadian National Railways at the several periods. I think, Mr. Chairman, when the minister introduces these amendments he should give consideration to bringing back to parliament the right to find out whether or not things are as they should be on the Canadian National Railways. The minister may say the committee does that. We have heard that story before. I have read almost all the committee reports, and the evidence taken. I noticed this: Whenever a question is asked that might furnish information which officials of the Canadian National Railways regard as not being in the public interest, and so often the public interest is apt to clash with the interests of officials of the Canadian National Railways, the information is not given.
Sir, I suggest, and I do so in the most serious way, that this is the picture of Canadian National Railways employees across Canada today. They are disturbed. They do not know where the axe is going to fall or when. They are afraid to get in touch with a member because so often they say, "We dare not do that." Much of the information comes in from sources that are anonymous, and therefore the information has to be checked. I ask the minister to say something to those railway employees that will restore their morale at this time.
Let me give you a recent example. Strong complaints have been made about R. F. Welch Limited-I think that is the name of the company. Mr. Gordon gave his promise that the things complained of would cease after March 31, but he did not say what year. Since March 31, 1,000 people who have been recently brought into Canada have been placed on two extra gangs out of Calgary, according to my information. What about the men who have been laid off? Why were they not given an opportunity, those who would be fitted for that work, to take this employment? A promise was given by Mr. Gordon that this was going to stop, that the injustices resulting from the hiring agreements of that company would be a thing of the past. Within the last two or three days one of the union representatives has been in touch with me concerning this question, and he simply requested that the matter be placed before the minister, and justice and equity asked for those who have been diligent and loyal servants of the Canadian National Railways,


Everywhere across the country there is fear. There is nothing that destroys morale more quickly, whether it is in corporations, in homes or anywhere else, than fear. I ask the minister whether he will do something to remove these clouds of fear that today hang over the Canadian National Railways employees, and give them a message of hope. At the same time he could once more give parliament the right to have information which, however concealed behind expressions such as have been used in recent months, is available and is simply being denied to parliament, as I see it, by the officials of the Canadian National Railways because they are afraid to have the information available. It is not going to help their competitors. How will it help their competitors to know how many employees have been laid off? The competitor allows it to be known how many employees have been laid off. Do that, and I say to the minister he will do a great deal to change deficits into surpluses. Today they fear. Today they are frustrated. Those are not of the elements that together give the cohesive unity and co-operation that will bring about at least a closer approximation of revenues with costs than has been the case during the last year.

Introducing as it does
legislation providing for an extension of the powers of the Canadian National Railways, particularly with a view to allowing the company to construct short lines without special permission, this resolution provides us with an opportunity of dealing with a subject which is of great interest to the northern part of the constituency of Roberval, which I represent in this house.
At the present time, this part of my constituency, including the municipalities of Dolbeau, Mistassini, St. Stanislas, St. Eugene d'Argentenay, Notre Dame de Lorette and Ste. Elizabeth de Proulx, plus part of this last named community and four others situated in the adjacent constituency of Lake St. John, is served through Dolbeau where the Canadian National Railways terminal is situated.
The economic advantage of a railway line and station to any community is well known. The value of such facilities can only be appreciated, in fact, by those who are deprived of them. Mistassini is in that case. Its trade, its postal service, its tourist facilities, the projected establishment of small industries, the existing industries and its agriculture, in a word, the economy of Mistassini in general is seriously handicapped by the lack of a railway.

The Mistassini area holds a population of
4,000	people, 3,000 of whom live in the town of the same name. Its economic life is based on forest products and the paper mill of the St. Lawrence Corporation, on trade of various kinds and on agriculture. A railway would strengthen the economic situation of the Mistassini area and would enable its industrious people to show what they can do. Ten years ago that district was contributing little to the economy of the district but its geographical location enabled it to assume an ever-increasing importance.
The bringing of the railway to Mistassini would require a two-mile extension of the line and the building of a bridge across the Mistassini river, which separates Dolbeau from Mistassini.
As they are made of wood and are more than 25 years old, the Dolbeau station and freight and express sheds are in need of major repairs, and as this project would probably mean the shifting of that station and those sheds to another part of the town of Dolbeau, the Canadian National should not miss the opportunity to rebuild those buildings which are out of date and not in keeping with such a fair town.
Fully aware of the needs of Mistassini and of the projects made for the future of that fast growing town, which now enjoys all essential services except those of railway transportation, I rely on the sympathetic consideration of this government and the Canadian National Railways for this project which I am anxious to see carried out, as are all my fellow citizens from Mistassini.

That is right. In the light of the figures appearing at page 2102 of Hansard for March 17, 1955 it appears that between August 1954 and January 1955 there was a drop in employment on the Canadian lines of the Canadian National Railways to the extent of 7,758 persons. It is a figure of that kind which makes the matter of lay-offs by the C.N.R. a serious one.
On that same page there are figures for the western region; and I note that in that area nearly half of this decline in employment has taken place. In that same period, from August 1954 to January 1955-and I understand all of these dates are at the middle of the month -there was a decline in employment of 3,844 persons.
I agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert that we should be able to get information far more readily than is the case. But even more important than getting the information is to have a stop put to this trend of lay-offs which is so serious for the men affected, as well as their families, not to mention the community as a whole.
I wish also to join in the protest made concerning the way in which the Canadian National Railways circumvent collective agreements with certain unions by contracting work out to R. F. Welch Limited. This is a serious matter. As hon. members may recall, I have asked the Minister of Labour in the house if his department could not go into this matter in some way. However, when I suggested that a commission of inquiry be established the minister replied that he did not feel there was anything his department could do. Meantime, employees of the Canadian National Railways doing this kind of work, and doing it under collective agreement, find that they are by-passed by a company which goes outside the terms of the agreement, when the work is let out by contract to the R. F. Welch company.
I wish also to say a few words about the policy of the Canadian National Railways with respect to its retired employees. Like the hon. member for Temiscouata, I feel I should relate my remarks to the legislation before the house. One of the acts to be consolidated is the Canadian National Railways Act; and I find that under the provisions of that act, by cross-reference to the Railway Act, the Canadian National Railways may set up and administer its pension plans. As hon. members know, there are a large number of retired C.N.R. employees on pensions that are ridiculously low. Again, if reference is made to Hansard, this time at pages 1762 and 1763 of March 7, 1955, it will be found that there are still ten retired C.N.R. employees on

Canadian National Railways pensions of less than $25 a month. In addition, there are 3,209 on pensions of only $25 a month. The tables on these pages are exhaustive, and I shall not attempt to repeat all the figures given.
However, may I say by way of summary that it appears there are a total of 19,460 retired C.N.R. employees who are on pensions, and that of that number there are 7,008 who are on pensions of less than $40 a month. Bearing in mind the fact that 3,209 are receiving only $25 a month, I suggest the time is long overdue for an increase in the pensions of those who draw only the basic pension, and for an adjustment in the pensions of those who are in the lower and middle brackets.
I regret the new Minister of Transport finds that he cannot say anything concerning these retired employees that is different from what his predecessor said. The main reply given to the associations who appear before the government from time to time is that these pensions are given and their amount determined by virtue of a contract. The argument is put forward that other persons who are drawing pensions under the terms of certain contracts are not having their pensions increased; and the question is then asked: Why should the government or why should the Canadian National Railways take action of that kind?
If it were true that no other group of pensioned employees had received any increase after going on pension, it would still not excuse the government from giving a lead in the matter. But as hon. members know, there are a number of instances where retired employees have been given increases even after going on pension. Certain levels of government in this country, as well as in other countries, have taken action along this line. For instance, in the last two or three months the retired teachers in this province of Ontario were given increases in their pensions. As a matter of fact the Canadian Pacific Railway makes a very slight addition to the pensions of those who are in the low brackets. I admit the supplement is small, and I admit also that the amount is taken off when the pensioner reaches the age of 70 and goes on old age security. But at least there are these examples of other employers who are trying to do something for their retired employees who are suffering because of what has happened in the meantime to the cost of living and to the value of the pension paid to these people.
After all, it should be recognized that if the Canadian National Railways is a great institution today, it is partly because of the work being done by those who are now its employees and partly because of the work


of those who have been its employees in the past. I submit it is not fair to these faithful servants of this government-owned railway, who have served in years gone by, to ask them to continue on pensions of the amounts I have repeated this afternoon.
I strongly urge the Minister of Transport to take a new look at this matter. I do not blame the minister, coming new to this portfolio, for following in the footsteps of his predecessor for a little while. A great many problems have been thrown on his doorstep, and there are many strings he has to pick up, with the result that it is only natural that he would carry on along the lines followed by his predecessor. The fact remains however that he is the person who is finally responsible, and that he is the person who is in parliament and who is answerable to members of parliament. I suggest therefore that he should take his own fresh look at the situation with a view to understanding just how serious the situation is for these people, and that he should try to find some way to do something about it, either by persuading the Canadian National Railways to act in the matter or by persuading his cabinet colleagues that the government should act so there would be brought about an increase in the pensions of these people who are in the lower brackets.
There were some other matters about which I wished to speak, but because so much time has been lost I shall only mention them in passing. I think it has not been good for the morale of Canadian National employees generally; I think it has not been good for the standing of Canadian National Railways in the eyes of the Canadian people, that the C.N.R. should have sold four of its institutions to be turned over to private hands. I refer to certain hotels and summer resorts. Likewise I feel that way about the decision of the management of the railway to lease the Queen Elizabeth hotel in Montreal to the Hilton chain. I have had a great many letters about these matters from citizens of Canada who wonder how these things gibe with the loyalty the Canadian government and the Liberal party are supposed to have to the principle of public ownership involved in the ownership by the people of Canadian National Railways.
These matters have been debated at length in this house, but I wanted to register my protest against what has been done in the context of steps that have been taken which have the effect of lowering the morale of Canadian National personnel and which affect the prestige and standing of the Canadian National Railways in the eyes of the Canadian people. So far as I am concerned and so

far as the members of this group are concerned, we are proud of the fact that we have a publicly owned railway system such as the Canadian National Railways, including not only its railroad operations but its various subsidiary operations. We do not want that excellent system to suffer in the way that we feel it has been suffering recently.
To me the things we have been discussing today are exceedingly important. I refer to the matters I have just mentioned in passing, and particularly to the pension position of those who are already retired and to the uncertainty and fear of losing their jobs that hang over so many of the employees. In the name of the prestige which the Canadian National Railways deserve in this country I call upon the government to review these matters and do something about them, particularly to raise the pensions of those in the lower brackets and to put an immediate stop to the lay-offs that have been taking place.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal briefly with two matters before the resolution passes. The hon. members for Prince Albert and Winnipeg North Centre have referred to the relationship between R. F. Welch Limited and the Canadian National Railways. A number of men employed by R. F. Welch Limited have been engaged in my constituency during the summer months, and there is a good deal of dissatisfaction


over the arrangements. It is very difficult for a member of parliament to find out how many are employed by R. F. Welch Limited at any given time, how much per day these men are paid, how much per day R. F. Welch Limited is paying for the services of the men.
At the beginning of this century we did take advantage of immigrants by asking them to do jobs that Anglo-Saxons disliked very much, and very low wages were paid. In the middle of the twentieth century I do not think it is good enough to bring immigrants to the country and ask them to compete with men who belong to unions, at wages which are apparently a great deal less than would be paid to Canadians undertaking that work. I have been told that R. F. Welch Limited makes up to $2 a day out of the labour of as many as 1,200 men at a given time. I do not know whether it is that much, or how much it is.
I realize that the men are under obligations to R. F. Welch Limited as a result of that company making it possible for them to be in Canada, but I think the parliament of Canada has a right to know all the details in connection with the relationships which exist between R. F. Welch Limited and the immigrants who come to Canada, and how much if anything the company is making per year as a result of the use of immigrants on the maintenance of way of the Canadian National Railways. I hope the minister will persuade the Canadian National Railways that these are matters of public concern. All the people of Canada have a right to be told exactly what are the details.
Earlier this afternoon the minister was kind enough to give the house some information regarding the operations of the two dieselized trains which started on Sunday. Earlier in the session I raised the question to find out why the Canadian Pacific had been able to announce the new faster service before the Canadian National Railways. The minister was able to draw my attention to the fact that both railways announced the service on the same date, but in the Gazette on that particular date the Canadian Pacific did announce in detail the saving in time that would be effected across the country, whereas the Canadian National Railways merely announced that they too were going to run a faster train.
The only reason I raise this matter is that throughout the years I have been a great advocate of public ownership. Having travelled on both railways, I think the Canadian National Railways has always given a comparable service. Some of my colleagues

are favourable to the Canadian Pacific, but both railways have given service of a very high order.
However, in recent months particularly there is a feeling that the Canadian National Railways are not getting a fair break. While it is true that the Canadian National Railways have a slightly longer run from Montreal to Vancouver, the difference is only 49 miles. Until Sunday the Canadian Pacific led the Canadian National Railways by only 15 minutes in the distance of 2,930 miles. If throughout the years the Canadian Pacific was able to drag along with just that difference, I cannot understand why now it becomes so much more hazardous for the Canadian National Railways to make the run across Canada in the same time or in 15 minutes less time than the Canadian Pacific.
I was a member of the railways and shipping committee some years ago when I believe it was Senator Reid, the member for New Westminster at that time, who expressed the opinion, when Mr. Vaughan was president of the railway, that the Canadian National could easily cut off 12 hours. I think Senator Reid said that coming east they were 12 hours late out of Edmonton but reached Ottawa on time.
I believe Mr. Vaughan admitted that the Canadian National Railways could cut their time by 12 hours, but he said that they wanted to arrive at Edmonton, Saskatoon, Winnipeg and other large centres at convenient hours, and there was not much point in going into Saskatoon at three o'clock in the morning or leaving Winnipeg in the middle of the night or reaching Toronto or Montreal at sometime between midnight and four o'clock in the morning. So those schedules were considered satisfactory.
It is hard for me to understand, if the Canadian Pacific is now making the run safely in the time they set out, why the Canadian National should have to take two hours and ten minutes longer. The Canadian Pacific will leave Montreal at one o'clock; business people will be able to have their lunch on the train, and in due course this train will reach Vancouver at 9.10 in the morning. So business people going from Montreal to Vancouver by train will have a half day in Montreal and a full day in Vancouver.
Those who travel via C.N.R. will have to hang around in Montreal until 3.25 in the afternoon and they will reach Vancouver at 1.45 p.m. on the same day the Canadian Pacific train will arrive at 9.10 a.m. So those who are travelling for business reasons will lose all the morning and it will be well on into the afternoon before they arrive in Vancouver. It would seem to me that the Canadian National should be able to make the
Canadian National Railways run across Canada as quickly as the Canadian Pacific, or certainly do better than run two hours and ten minutes slower.
It has always been argued that the Canadian National has a better roadbed. I came back from Winnipeg at Easter on the Canadian Pacific. I have been a C.N.R. man all my life, but I wanted to see what the Canadian Pacific was like. I was able to see the new dome cars, and they are very attractive. Those who have travelled over the C.P.R. will agree that there are a great many sharp curves as you follow the north shore of Lake Superior. Those who have travelled across the Rockies will also agree that the Canadian National has a much better crossing through the mountains. speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Diefen-baker for the second reading of Bill No. 186, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext: While I have not checked the matter, the hon. member for Prince Albert will permit me to say that, if he speaks now, he will close the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment was introduced on March 18 in order to cover the matter of the pollution of interprovincial streams. Because of the long period that has elapsed 
since its introduction I should like to refer to it for the purpose of having it on the record. It reads:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to a fine of ten thousand dollars for a first offence and of twenty thousand dollars for a second offence, or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.
Such punishment, of course, would be in accordance with the provisions of the Criminal Code with relation to summary conviction penalties.
I want to thank all those who have spoken on this amendment. Generally speaking I think there has been agreement that the pollution of our interprovincial streams is a matter of ever-increasing seriousness, and that across Canada in practically every province the waterways are becoming polluted to a degree that will ensure, in a matter of a generation, the almost complete destruction of their usefulness for domestic or manufacturing purposes, unless action is taken.
The Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Garson), in dealing with the matter, contended that a question such as this could be dealt with on the basis of co-operation as between province and province. In the past few weeks I have had from various parts of this country considerable correspondence indicating that this problem is national in scope and that federal action is necessary to meet it and to punish those who would destroy for the great body of the Canadian people the usefulness of the God-given rivers which supply our manufacturing industries and are also a source of our domestic water supply.
There was a request on the part of various fish and game organizations for legislation such as is embodied in this amendment. A recent example, to which I shall but allude, was the occurrence on the North Saskatchewan river. As a result of the dumping of effluents by Canadian Chemical Company Limited into the North Saskatchewan river at a point east of Edmonton, the waters of the river were rendered unusable for a period of three months by the cities of Battleford and Prince Albert, the town of The Pas, and by people living between Edmonton and The Pas.
To summarize the minister's stand, he said first of all that there was no need for this legislation inasmuch as the amendments to the Criminal Code recently passed by par-

liament, which became law on April 1, would cover the situation. When the minister referred to that point I asked him a simple question, as is found at page 2504 of Hansard for March 29. The minister was turning to another point, and at that time I said:
Before the minister goes on with that, will he permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
It has to do with the suggestion he made the other day that the new section is different in import and purport from the old section.
Then I read the old section, which was as follows:
A common nuisance is an unlawful act or omission to discharge a legal duty, which act or omission endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or by which the public are obstructed in the exercise or enjoyment of any right common to all His Majesty's subjects.
That section had been in the law for many years. That was the section at the time the event took place to which I referred a minute ago, when the North Saskatchewan river was to all intents and purposes but a floating sewer of effluents that had been dumped into it by an industrial concern east of Edmonton. The amendment which became law this year reads as follows:
(2) For the purposes of this section every one commits a common nuisance who does an unlawful act or fails to discharge a legal duty and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or
(b)	obstructs the public in the exercise or enjoyment of any right that is common to all the subjects of Her Majesty in Canada.
Then I asked the minister this question:
What is different in these two sections?
The minister replied quite frankly and said:
If I understand my hon. friend's question correctly he is asking me whether I contend that the new section differs in any point of substance from the old section. I agree that there is no substantial difference between them. I did not argue that there was.
However, a reading of his earlier remarks would indicate that one of the reasons he gave for opposing the amendment I suggested was that the new amendment to the Criminal Code now in effect would make it a punishable offence to destroy the waters of any river, so far as use by the public was concerned, in the manner which was in evidence on the North Saskatchewan river.
Then the minister took up another line, as I saw it, and stated that the amendment now before the house did not cover municipalities dumping sewage into rivers. I am not so sure he was right in that regard, because it would make it an offence for any person to dump raw sewage into a river. However, to
Criminal Code
make assurance doubly sure I asked the minister this question, as is found at the top of page 2507:
If my amendment were altered to include municipalities which put raw sewage into rivers and thereby contribute to the pollution, would the minister then accept it?
This was his answer:
I am now expressing my own personal views. I would not accept it because I would think if that were done it would expose a great many municipalities, including perhaps the city of Ottawa, to prosecution in police court, which prosecution would in my judgment contribute very little, if anything at all, to the solution of the problem with which the hon. member is attempting to deal. In other words, I do not think police court prosecutions are a solution for river pollution.
In other words the minister first took two stands, and when faced with an answer to both those stands he finally took the position that he did not believe prosecution was the best means to prevent wrongs such as were committed against the peoples of the cities of Prince Albert and Battleford and the town of The Pas. I think the best summary of the situation was given in an editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of April 15, 1954. After reviewing the situation prevailing on the North Saskatchewan river the editorial went on to say:
Hitherto there has been a tendency to take the protests of the people of Prince Albert and Battleford much too lightly: to regard the unpleasantness of their water as little more than annoyance; even, on occasion to treat the efforts of elected representatives to obtain a solution as mere politicking. Why this should have been the case, why the right of human beings to water as pure as nature and normal circumstances offer should have been so disregarded, we don't know. But we suspect the fisheries report

That was the report issued a few days earlier by the director of fisheries of Saskatchewan.
-will put a different complexion on the matter; and for that reason above all it is to be welcomed.
Then there is the following:
To this end it may be necessary to widen the scope of federal law so that it covers a broader range of types and effects of pollution-so that it is more in accord with conditions likely to crop up in our industrializing age. But law is only a deterrent, not a preventative. Something more is needed, something which will meet the difficulties caused by the fact that pollution of waters in one province may, as in the case of the North Saskatchewan, produce harmful results in another. Here we believe the establishment of an agency patterned on the prairie provinces water board or, for a start, an extension of that board's powers, offers the best solution.
Well, a board has been set up. In addition, as the Star-Phoenix editorial points out, teeth should be put in the law. As the law is at the present time, the opinion of the best counsel procurable was to the effect that the section did not permit of any successful

Criminal Code
prosecution being launched against the wrongdoer. The same situation prevails in other parts of the country.

speechtext: Was that opinion of counsel, to which he has just referred, based upon the fact that counsel was not assured that there was sufficient evidence upon which a conviction could be obtained?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
No, far from it. The question whether there is sufficient evidence is for the court. What was submitted to counsel-and by "counsel" I refer to the legal representatives who were consulted-was based upon the premise that the city of Prince Albert or any of the other municipalities had sufficient evidence upon which to establish the identity of the wrongdoer, and the opinion was that the section in question did not permit of a successful prosecution. I think it is pretty obvious when the section is read. It says:
A common nuisance is an unlawful act or omission to discharge a legal duty, which act or omission endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or by which the public are obstructed in the exercise or enjoyment of any right common to all Her Majesty's subjects.
My hon. friend says, as I understand his argument, that the unlawful act consists of the breach of a provincial health statute. Once that breach is established it gives rise to a prosecution under the section in question, as amended in the present Criminal Code, because of the fact that the doing of the act in question contrary to the health act of an individual province gives a right of action.
The opinion of counsel was that such was not the fact, and that the unlawful act as comprehended by the section in question must be an unlawful act within the meaning of the Criminal Code itself. Indeed, counsel gave legal precedents to support that viewpoint, and gave us their opinion that there was no right of criminal action to prosecute the wrongdoers who, for a period of three months, flouted the comfort of tens of thousands of people. I mention that not in order to bring forward this amendment as a means of protecting only the people of Saskatchewan along the North Saskatchewan river alone, but the people of several provinces along the course traversed by that river.
I feel that we in Canada face a problem which will have to be met. In the United States it is being met, but in Canada it is being by-passed by both parliament and the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.}
legislatures. I am not condemning the government of Alberta in any way when I say this, but according to the representatives of the government of Saskatchewan the government of Alberta did not take a very distinct interest in assuring that the waters, after they left Alberta, would be suitable for consumption in the other provinces the river traversed. After all, a number of great industries have been established in Edmonton, and certainly Alberta will do nothing to assist the other provinces in preserving the waters of the river unless the federal authority joins in and places teeth in the Criminal Code of this country, without which there is no protection to anyone living in a province through which a river passes on in turn to another province.

Well, my hon. friends keep on interrupting and making these loose statements, but the record stands. My hon. friends are opposed to this amendment because they do not want teeth put in the legislation. They realize that one, and possibly more, of their industries in Alberta would be subject to prosecution. Naturally, with the solicitude that the provincial attitude gives them, they oppose the amendment in this form because it would place teeth in the law and would preserve us under the law from pollution, by making it possible to punish effectively those who deliberately pollute interprovincial streams and thereby deny the use of the waters of those streams to other provinces.
Having said that, and having pointed out the dangers, I would hope to receive support from various hon. members. In particular I would refer to the hon. member for Ros-thern (Mr. Tucker), who on April 2, 1954, indicated in the house that the pollution of rivers is a crime under the present nuisance section of the Criminal Code, and that if it was not a crime, then in his opinion under the law it should be made one.
It is a crime to place in rivers anything that will interfere with the lives of fish. Under the Fisheries Act that is set out as a pseudo-crime; but, as yet, it is no crime to put interprovincial rivers and waterways in

Criminal Code
a condition whereby they cannot be used by humans. It is because of that, sir, that this amendment was drafted in a form that the law officers of the crown believed would cover the situation, a form which in my opinion places in the hands of those who are wronged the power to launch prosecutions against those interests, however powerful they may be. It provides suitable and heavy penalties against any industries or other bodies anywhere that would flagrantly destroy the water resources of the nation in interprovincial streams.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find myself in a somewhat peculiar position, because the hon. member who spoke previously said that he thought any further remarks on this matter might be tempered with common sense. I find that I have to judge my common sense as compared with that of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken.
I realize that this debate has been very wide. It has covered perhaps the whole gamut of the Canadian National Railways. But there is a matter of very great importance which I should like to bring to the attention of this house at this time, and I hope it will not be completely out of place. As a matter of fact, when I look at the resolution I see that it has to deal with the construction of short lines without specific parliamentary authority, and also authority to operate motor vehicles.
I should like to say only a few words in connection with the commuter systems in this country. First of all I should like to speak generally, and then I should like to come down to the specific situation which I find in my county and the county of Peel.
If I may be permitted to say so, the general principle is perhaps that the Canadian National Railways has arrived at a point in its outlook and in the general business practice of this country when it must decide whether it may have to change its methods of carrying on railroading. It has always been assumed that the long runs were the ones that paid in this country, but I notice that not so long ago before the committee the chairman of the company made the suggestion that it might be considered feasible on the part of the Canadian National Railways to look into the matter of the short interurban runs, and to deal with suburban services.
It is exactly that of which I should like to speak. It may well be that we have arrived at that stage of railroading. I should like the minister to note the lack of public support for this railway and the fact that the Canadian National Railways is now showing a deficit. If we are cognizant of the rights of the people of this country we should not be asking for an extension of this service, and I do not want to be placed in the position of asking for that. But I do say, Mr. Chairman, that the time may have arrived for us to consider the carrying on of interurban communication, particularly having in mind that many parts of this country are becoming thickly populated. People are coming into large centres for industrial reasons, and they are finding that as the population grows they have to live farther out. They
Canadian National Railways have to come into the great cities or industrial centres to work or carry on business.
In my county of Halton-and may I speak too of the county of Peel, with deference to the hon. member for Peel-we have this situation. We have Toronto itself and metropolitan Toronto. I think I can safely say that thousands of people have gone from the centre of what used to be considered Toronto to live out in the southern part of the county of Peel and the southern part of the county of Halton. They go back daily into Toronto and nearby centres to work in factories or offices, or to carry on their business, whatever it may be.
That area from Oakville to Toronto, a distance of 21 miles, has a population of 700,000 people including outer Toronto proper. A very large number of those people are commuting every day to Toronto and nearby from Oakville, from Clarkson, from Port Credit, from Mimico and all those surrounding centres; and, of course, they are coming home at night. Serving that area we have actually only two great highways, the lake shore highway, which is rather antiquated, and the Queen Elizabeth way. Every morning and every evening you see those highways completely and totally congested. It takes about an hour, an hour and a half, or even two hours at times to get into the city or get home, to say nothing of the danger that is created.
For some time we have been asking for commuter service over the Canadian National Railways, because that is the line that runs through Oakville, Lome Park, Port Credit and so on. What I am saying applies not only to my area but generally to the areas of many hon. members of this house. We are asking that something be done to increase or better these services.
The service at present is this. In the morning we have two trains-they are not actually commuter trains but merely trains that run from Hamilton and pick up people at these various points-that arrive in Toronto before nine o'clock. We have another that arrives between nine and ten o'clock, but it is not a commuter train at all. In the evening, leaving the city, we have three trains that leave after five and arrive by 7.30, which is a very late hour.
Although I have not made an exact survey of the other services throughout Canada, I think perhaps the most nearly comparable and most outstanding service is that at Montreal. It is an old city and the people there have been given this service for many years. In place of two morning trains I find that they have ten modern trains that arrive in Montreal before nine o'clock. In place of

Canadian National Railways three evening trains they have some twelve trains. Then of course they have trains interspersed during the day and later on into the night.
I am not saying this is absolutely correct, but I am told that the population in my area, in the counties of Halton and Peel, is now almost twice that being served in the same area down near Montreal. In addition, the cars we are using on what might be called our sham commuter service are old. They are not up to date. The service is not speedy. There are great delays.
The fare has been raised by 75 per cent since last September. In other words, where we were paying $10 for 40 rides down to the end of the county, we are now paying $17.50 for 40 rides. There has been no improvement in service, although there has been some improvement in the cars and equipment. By September 1 there will be another 25 per cent raise and we shall then have had a raise of 100 per cent. On the other hand, down in the Montreal area I believe there has been a raise of about 50 per cent.
We are not finding fault with the Canadian National Railways in connection with what they decide to do in the Montreal area as to the number of trains, the price they charge or anything of that kind. What we should like to have is some parity of service, some recognition of the fact that we are a growing area and that we have a great problem which is becoming greater every day.
In all fairness may I say this. Personally I believe that the whole of the people of this country are responsible for this railway. We have been to the commission and we have been to the president. Sometimes I think, as was said this afternoon, that the president owns the railway when he is giving orders but the people own the railway when it comes to paying the bills.
What I should like to suggest to the minister, if he would take it into consideration, is not that extra trains be put on at this time. Perhaps we cannot afford that. Perhaps the Canadian National is being pressed. I suggest that he go into this whole question of the future service of the Canadian National Railways to this country, with particular reference to the conditions in these thickly populated areas.
We would ask that this one thing be considered by the minister. There are several of what we call flyers, to use common terminology. For instance, there is the Chicago flyer, which very often has to stop at Oakville, and very often it is flagged down at Clarkson. Without losing much time or without much loss with regard to service I should


think that flyer could stop and pick up these commuters. Going out from Toronto in the evening, between 4.30 and seven o'clock, are two such trains that also could be used for this purpose. That is all we are asking at this time.
This is a pressing problem, and one that is growing greater all the time. Without offering any criticism of what the company or the government does for other centres, we ask that they consider the problem we have with this growing population and growing industrialization. We ask that, if it is at all possible, we be brought to parity with other large centres in this country. We also ask that consideration be given to making some use of the service that is already available there. We suggest that it be opened up to the commuters of my county and, if I may say so with respect, those of the county of Peel, because this matter is a great problem to them as well.

Mr. Chairman, I would think there is a great deal of material that could either be discussed on this resolution or left to the estimates. Much of what I might have said I shall leave to the estimates. I shall not, for example, discuss at any length the feeling I experienced over the last week end when that magnificent Canadian Pacific transcontinental train, the Canadian, with its dome cars, started on its way across the country with public attention focused on it, everybody thinking about it and reading about it, and press representatives clamouring to get on it, when at the same time the equipment of the new C.N.R. train definitely, and regrettably, had to take second place. In fact, so much did it have to take second place that the C.N.R. had to run a special train on Saturday to give the press people an opportunity to view the new equipment, because they were all going to ride on the new C.P.R. train Sunday night. I think things like that are perhaps much better left to the estimates when we can discuss them in detail.
But, Mr. Chairman, when we look at the Canadian National Railways it does stir our imagination more than a little bit. When you think of the history of these lines, somewhat checkered at times, you cannot help

but feel that there is a challenge to Canadians to take this tremendous transportation system and do everything each one of us can to see that it attains and retains the preeminent position it should rightly have.
I should like to refer to the people who work for the railway, and I am not talking now about the minister or the president of the railway but of what we sometimes think of as the little people, the men up and down the line, track walkers, engineers, conductors, the people in the offices, all those who are going to be affected directly or indirectly by the legislation presented to the house. When we think of them and realize the life of service they have given to the organization and the tremendous job they have done in working for it, I think we should all feel a sense of gratitude and want to do anything we can to help them.
Actually it was not my intention to intervene in this debate at all until I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Albert this afternoon. They struck a responsive chord in me, because I could not help thinking that if the hon. member for Prince Albert, in addition to all the experience he has had in the house, had had the experience of being present at the sessions of the railways and shipping committee a few weeks ago he would have been even more vehement in his protests and, if it is possible, even more definite in his views.
When I look at the resolution before us it brings to mind the complex problems of the Canadian National Railways, and one cannot help but have a great sense of sympathy for the president of the road in his job of trying to balance the financial dictates of his vast empire with the reasonable demands of the tens of thousands of people working with the railway for job security and a decent living. I imagine that is the sort of thing that must weigh heavily on him at all times, and it is in regard to that aspect of his work that I think those of us in the house must have very great sympathy for him.
But, Mr. Chairman, in considering this legislation, which is to be referred to the standing committee, may I say now that I have no sympathy whatsoever with the attitude of either the president of the company or the minister in their appearances before the committee on railways and shipping and the reactions they displayed there. I bring up this point now because I believe the attitudes they revealed there should not be repeated, particularly in the present instance, when we are going to engage in far-reaching studies of this vast enterprise and with all the resources available to us attempt to benefit it and move it even further ahead.
Canadian National Railways
To point out the sort of thing which I think should not be repeated in the committee may I refer to three cases of arrant disregard, in my estimation, of the purposes of the house and its committees. The first one to which I turn my attention concerns the president of the road himself. Incidentally, all three instances had to do with the consideration of the C.N.R. hotels, although they occurred at widely scattered intervals during the work of the committee. It puts us in the almost untenable position of having answers to certain points ruled out.
Having said that, I would turn for a moment to what from past experience I would judge the minister's attitude to be on legislation such as this. I have not detected any great sympathy on the part of the minister for any suggestion that a sincere attempt be made to examine into the Canadian National Railways, and to obtain from such examination facts upon which the consideration of particular instances might be based.
I think that has a very great bearing on this resolution. If time and again we are


going to come up against this wall of secrecy, this unrelenting hot air curtain as I referred to it at one time, on the part of the government, beyond which is hidden information, it will make it extremely difficult for us to go ahead. For example, there was this statement in committee by the minister:

The minister was referring to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. He seemed to think there was something wrong in a committee of this house passing judgment on the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. I think at that point we diametrically part company. It would seem to me that in certain cases committees of this house are formed primarily for that very purpose, to examine the acts of government departments, to examine the acts of subsidiary government bodies, to examine groups to which legislative or executive power has been delegated, and then come to our own conclusions as to whether or not they have properly fulfilled that trust.
I cannot criticize too strongly the attitude of any minister of the crown who may come before a committee and indicate that that committee should not pass judgment or by inference examine actions within the field of study which has been delegated to it.

While he did not mention the railway line, it was a boat train that met the Cunard liner Scythia in Halifax, and his complaints were recorded. I might say they prompted me to rise this evening to make some reference to an experience of my own several years ago.
When Mrs. Lennard and I returned from the coronation in late June, 1953, we landed at Quebec from another Cunard liner, the Samaria. We had our reservations on a Canadian National boat train from Quebec to Toronto. There were two trains; one took passengers to Montreal and points north, I believe, and the train on which we were booked by-passed Montreal and proceeded to Toronto. That train was about the filthiest and most outmoded affair on which I had ever travelled. You can imagine my shame when all these people from other countries- England and Scotland in particular-had to travel under such conditions. It did not bother me too much personally because, being a Canadian, I had travelled under all sorts of conditions; but I did feel thoroughly ashamed on that occasion that these people from other countries should be welcomed on such an outfit.
On that train several of the sleepers had the old gas lamps. There was not a uniform diner; there was a club car where meals were served by a crew that was certainly far from perfection. Even after we had entered Ontario and were west of Cornwall, at the evening meal, that crew was still charging Quebec hospital tax, at which I protested, of course. That was after we had been in Ontario for over an hour. That is

how little they knew of the proper methods in travelling across the country.
I had forgotten this incident and had passed it off as a mistake, as probably it was a time when they had not the proper cars or accommodation, and I thought it was something that could not be helped. But when the hon. member for Simcoe North brought up his experience of only two months ago on another boat train serving the Cunard line, I thought it was about time something was heard of my experience of several years ago. If that is the pattern the Canadian National railways have adopted in meeting our visitors from abroad and in serving the Cunard line, it is about time that pattern was changed.
