I wish to discuss several points under this resolution, and the one I wish to discuss particularly is the sale of the four C.N.R. hotels, the one in Port Arthur, the one in Brandon, the one in Minaki, and the one in Pictou.
After a great deal of delving and with extreme difficulty the information was pried -and I use the word advisedly-from the management of the C.N.R. that these hotels had been disposed of for the sum of $915,000. Let us examine for a moment the method of sale that was adopted. Do not forget that these hotels were the property of the Canadian people, and as such it was incumbent on those who are supposed to represent the best interests of the Canadian people to get the best possible price.
The method adopted in selling these hotels was to call for tenders. Has anybody ever heard of a commercial concern with a similar merchandising problem on its hands calling for tenders? As a matter of fact these properties, I submit, ought to have been placed in the hands of skilled real estate merchandisers, and they should have examined the market and decided on possible purchasers. In the case of one of these hotels, the one at Port Arthur, an attorney informs me that he had a client who approached him and suggested that he had heard that this hotel was for sale and he wondered how much they might

take for it. He intimated he had heard that it might be purchased for approximately $400,000. In regard to the second hotel, the one in Brandon, I have had representations made to me that a number of people would have been prepared to pay a quarter of a million dollars for this hotel.
That makes a total of $650,000. I do not know the appraised value or the price or the cost factor with regard to the hotel at Minaki, but I do know that the golf course alone cost the Canadian people a million dollars. There was information available some years ago that an American person wondered if he could have bought the hotel for $2 million, but he was advised that it was very unlikely that he could have done so. I know nothing about Pictou lodge.
In view of all this it seems only reasonable to think that if competent real estate salesmanship had been exercised a great deal more money could have been obtained for the Canadian people for this asset which was in their possession.
I leave that matter, Mr. Chairman, and proceed to deal with the question of C.N.R. pensions which my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already mentioned with regard to this question of pensions, many of which are on the basis of equal contributions by the employee and the railroad, it seems to me that the employee has paid into the fund in dollars that were worth 100 cents or in excess of 100 cents, and is now being paid off in dollars that are worth approximately 50 cents. This is definitely ^ a responsibility of the government. For this reason I would suggest that the government has a moral responsibility to see to it that these people are paid their pensions in com the same as that with which they paid for them.
The government may say that this is the fate of everybody who buys pensions. That is true. If one buys a pension from an insurance company one must take the same risk. But I would point out that the insurance company has nothing to do with the value of the Canadian dollar, whereas the government has a great deal to do with it. Consequently I would submit that there is a good case for the government to make adjustments in these pensions so as to compensate people for the depreciation of the dollar, which is a government responsibility.
That is my argument. I would say this is a fundamental question in the Canadian economy which, of course, goes far beyond the question of C.N.R. pensions. But at the same time the C.N.R., as an agency of government, has a definite responsibility to see

At the same time perhaps he could also indicate whether the government intends at this session to bring in any legislation having to do with agreed charges. As the minister knows, a report by Mr. Turgeon was tabled just a few weeks ago. Both the railways and

Canadian National Railways the motor carriers are vitally interested in what is to be done as a result of that report. Perhaps the minister could tell us this evening whether there is to be any legislation at this session. It would seem to me that matter would be extremely material so far as the railways operating motor vehicles is concerned.
Then the third point has to do with the abandonment of lines. Apparently there have been quite a few instances in which the railways have abandoned lines in recent months, and there is a good deal of uneasiness over this policy. Will the changes that are contemplated in this legislation make it easier for the C.N.R. to abandon lines? At the present time they can do so only with the approval of the board of transport commissioners. That means there is an opportunity for the people affected to protest.
In his explanation the other night the minister pointed out that power was being taken to extinguish the charters of subsidiary companies of the Canadian National Railways. That raises the possibility that in this way the abandoning of lines will be facilitated. I would ask the minister to give us an explanation on that point.
Then finally there is this point. Last night the minister said the new legislation would consolidate, among other things, certain provisions which were found in the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act. That act, of course, has to do with the two railways. I do not quite understand how part of that act can be taken out and put into a Canadian National act without affecting the Canadian Pacific Railway. This act to which I am referring was designed to bring about cooperation between our two great railways. It seems odd that some portion can now be taken from that act and be put in a Canadian National statute without the Canadian Pacific Railway being brought into the Canadian National statute as well. I may be quite wrong in thinking that such could be the case, but I would ask the minister to explain to the committee what the result of the proposed legislation will be in respect of this particular act.

The C.N.R. and the C.P.R. operate motor vehicles now, and I am wondering whether, if the C.N.R. gets permission through parliament to operate motor vehicles, the railway may be in the position of being able to override the provisions of any province regarding the issuance of licences for motor vehicles. As the situation stands today, if the railways want to operate motor vehicles in the city of Calgary, for example, they have to get a licence from the provincial government, and they must show need before any more licences are issued so the industry will not be overcrowded, and in order to satisfy other precautions laid down by the province.
It was pointed out to us by Mr. Gordon, president of the C.N.R., that the railways were now using the operation of motor vehicles to extend, as he put it, competition with the trucking industry of Canada. The railways are operating specially equipped flat cars by which they can carry their trailer trucks by rail for long distances. As a result they are hoping to provide keener opposition to the trucking business of the Dominion of Canada. That is a point about which I think we as members of parliament should be very cautious. The railways are now hauling goods in their trailer trucks on these specially equipped flat cars at ridiculously low rates. In fact it has been suggested to me by some of the large trucking companies that the railways are carrying these goods on these piggy-back cars, as they are called, at less than cost.
I believe the Railway Act specifically states that no railway shall haul goods at less than cost. When I asked the president of Canadian National Railways about that point he said-I forget the exact words he used-that they were making some profit but he was unprepared to say how much it was. There is a great deal of conjecture about whether or not the railways are actually hauling this traffic at less than cost, and there is very great national danger in that operation. We know that the railways are entering into agreed charge arrangements. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned

that a few moments ago and expressed the hope the minister would elaborate on, it. I also would like the minister to deal with it.
The railways are now entering into agreed charge contracts. They enter into an agreement with a large manufacturing concern or a large retail store such as Eaton's, Simpson's or Simpsons-Sears, under which they haul large quantities of goods for these large companies either at cost or very close to it. This puts these large retail concerns in the position of more than competing with our small merchants. It should be understood that the small merchants provide far more of the services required by the country than do the large manufacturers or retail merchants such as Eaton's, Simpson's or Simpsons-Sears.
By entering into agreed charge contracts the railways are assisting the large chain stores not only to meet the competition of the small merchants throughout the country but to eliminate them. It is dangerous to allow the railways to operate motor vehicles and enter into these outrageous agreed charge contracts. We might as well face the fact it is not the intention of the railways to meet the competition of trucks but to eliminate the truck as a competitor. We might as well recognize that now. Those of us in western Canada and the maritime provinces are more concerned over this type of so-called competition than those who live in central Canada, where other forms of competition bring about a lowering of railway charges.
I am very much concerned about this matter, and I ask the minister to comment at some length on the statements I have made, particularly pertaining to the operation of motor vehicles by railway companies and the use of agreed charges,

The hon. member for Mackenzie referred to the speed of the two transcontinental trains. I see that took up from
Canadian National Railways page 66 to page 69. I am quite sure members of the committee will realize that if I were to do justice to the management of Canadian National Railways I should read from the evidence extracts to show what the president of the railway said in reply to questions on various subjects.
I think that these few examples are sufficient to show how unwise it would be for me to attempt to deal with each of these various questions which I think, strictly speaking, refer to the operation of the railway and the policies of the management but not to the statutes governing the railway itself.
There have been, however, a number of points raised in connection with the legislation itself, and I should like to try to deal with these as summarily and as simply as possible. The first of the important questions raised was that concerning the short branch lines. As I understand the law at present, Canadian National Railways requires parliamentary approval for two aspects of branch line construction. First of all it must have an appropriation or an amount included in its capital budget with the approval of parliament; and secondly, it must have specific legislative approval of the branch line which it proposes to construct. Other railways in Canada which are governed in this respect by the Railway Act are subject only to this disability, that provided the branch line does not exceed six miles in length all they require is the approval of the board of transport commissioners.
In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred a moment ago, the Canadian Pacific enjoys a rather peculiar situation. Under the agreement which 1 believe was ratified by parliament in 1885 the Canadian Pacific has the power, without either parliamentary approval or the approval of the board of transport commissioners, to construct branch lines from its main line-I understand that refers to the portion of its main line lying to the west of Callander, Ontario. The position of the Canadian National is that it does not enjoy the powers with regard to the construction of short lines that are enjoyed by all the other railways in Canada governed by the Railway Act.
As I said last night and again this afternoon, the proposed legislation is to limit the short line provision to those lines not exceeding six miles in length. The purpose which the management of Canadian National Railways has in mind is the necessity of meeting the demands of industry for lines that do not rate as short spurs but which have a length of up to six miles. The management hope that if this power were given they would be able

Canadian National Railways promptly to build these short lines when required. At the moment the situation is that although there may be funds in the railway's capital budget available for the construction of such a short line, let us say five miles in length intended to serve some industry, if the application to the railway for the construction of the line is made after parliament has adjourned then the railway is in the position of being unable to respond to the demand until it has parliamentary authority to construct the line.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it would be desirable that Canadian National Railways should be freed from this disability, and that it is not unreasonable to give it the power to build these short lines. This is particularly true if members of the committee will bear in mind that the necessary funds must be appropriated by parliament and included in the capital budget, so the freedom of action which Canadian National will obtain under the proposed legislation is less than that enjoyed by other railway companies, and much less than that enjoyed by the Canadian Pacific.
I should like to be fair in my explanations to the committee, Mr. Chairman, on that one point. This afternoon the hon. member for Macleod spoke of the facility with which the Canadian National could expropriate land required for its right of way. I believe I should be fair to the committee by saying that the Canadian National has what I think ought to be regarded as much more effective powers of expropriation than the other railways have. In other words, as I understand it, under the statute the Canadian National can deposit a plan and thereby become immediately the owner of the land affected, whereas as I understand it under the Railway Act there is no provision for obtaining immediate possession. I believe the other railways, in the matter of expropriation, are under some slight disability in comparison with Canadian National Railways.
I do feel that the request of the management to be empowered to construct a line up to six miles in length for industrial purposes 's reasonable and removes a disability which ought now to be removed in the interests of the operation of the railway.
The next question which was raised concerning the provisions of the bill was that respecting motor vehicles. As I endeavoured to explain last night the railway now has powers through subsidiary companies to operate motor vehicles. They have been under this disability in the past, that at times when consideration has been given to the abandonment of a short line the railway has been in the rather peculiar position before the board of transport commissioners of being unable
[Mr. Marler.l

to offer, on behalf of the railway company itself, to undertake to provide motor service in lieu of a passenger train. They have had to produce the undertaking of some subsidiary to provide that service. They have no power to operate motor vehicles, so they are unable to give a formal undertaking that they will establish a motor service as an alternative to the train service they propose to abandon.
At all events I should like to assure the members of the committee, and particularly the hon. member for Bow River, that there is no intention on the part of the government, in adding to the powers of the railway that of owning and operating motor vehicles, to make any sinister change of policy. We merely intend to make a change which will enable the railways, in effect, to do through the parent company what they have been doing already through subsidiary companies.
There is no suggestion either that in granting this power the railway shall be free from the necessity of complying with the requirements of provincial governments so far as provincial laws apply to the operation of motor vehicles owned by the company.

Then, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and also the hon. member for Bow River referred to the question of agreed charges as having some connection with the power to operate motor vehicles to be provided for in the bill. I would like to assure both hon. members that there is certainly not in my mind any connection between these two subjects. In relation to legislation concerning agreed charges, and the possibility of its being brought before parliament at this session, at the present time I can merely say the matter is under active consideration, and that as soon as a decision has been reached by the government it will be announced. If it is intended to introduce legislation at this session I take it that due notice will be given of that fact.
I do not think, however, that the question of agreed charges of itself really relates to the management of the railroad, in the sense in which I am using the term at the moment. We are concerned with the legislative provisions which govern the railways, and I think I can assure my hon. friend from Vancouver-Quadra that nothing in the bill which it is proposed to introduce will refer specifically to agreed charges, or deprive the railways of the right to take advantage of the statute as it exists at the present time or as it may exist after amendment, if amendments are thought necessary.
Then the question was also raised as to whether the provisions of the bill would make it easier to effect the abandonment of lines. I think I should answer that by saying that inasmuch as none of the amendments to the various enactments which it is proposed to make deal with the subject of the abandonment of lines, I do not think I should say that the bill would make it either easier or more difficult. I think possibly if it were easier it would merely be in the context upon which I touched briefly a moment ago, in that it might conceivably facilitate abandonment if the railway were itself able to undertake to supply motor vehicle service in lieu of train service, and to do so formally in its own name rather than in the name of a subsidiary. But with that exception I can see nothing in the proposed legislation which makes the abandonment of lines either easier or more difficult.
Canadian National Railways
With regard to the provisions concerning the abandonment or surrender of charters of constituent corporations, I am sure the hon. member will find, when the bill is brought down, that the dispositions are procedural in character, and not intended to affect the rights of any person or community which might be served by the constituent company. I take it that it is the intention, where a company or charter has served its full purpose and has run out its time, so to speak, that there should be a simple method of putting an end to the legal existence of the company concerned. I think the hon. member will find that the provisions of the bill deal merely with the question of procedure rather than with the questions of substance that I think he has in mind.
Another point raised was in connection with the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra raised the point as to whether there could be partial repeal of a statute which appeared to concern both of the great railways. I may assure him that it is not intended that the whole act should be repealed, but there are parts or sections of some of these joint statutes which apply to the Canadian National Railways and which can be repealed without in any way affecting the fabric of the remainder of the statutes. In fact I think if my hon. friend from Vancouver-Quadra will examine what I said last night he will see that I merely mentioned that act as being one of those which have to be consulted when someone wishes to have the complete total of all the enactments which apply to the Canadian National Railways, and there are parts which properly may be consolidated into a bill affecting the powers and rights of the Canadian National Railways.
One other point was raised by the hon. member for Bow River. He spoke of the question of the transporting of goods by the railways at rates which were less than cost. I take it his comment applies to the tariffs which have been set up between Montreal and Toronto particularly, and which are competitive. I am told that these rates do provide a small margin of profit to the railways, and that they are not operating this service at a loss. In any event, that is really outside the scope of this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes which remain of this sitting it would not be possible, of course, to deal with the bill which has now been in our hands for some three weeks. The best I can hope to do this evening, I think, is to make a few remarks, and I can continue those remarks when this house sits again.
I might make a few comments on the statement just made by the minister, and I might say in that regard that I had thought the minister would pick up tonight some of the remarks which he rather cut short at the conclusion of the resolution stage. At that time he implied that he would use the next opportunity to answer more fully some of the comments which had been made at the resolution stage. Many of us were glad to welcome that arrangement because we thought that in the meantime we would have the bill in our hands and be prepared to go ahead with discussion.
However, tonight the minister has made one remark with which I feel I must deal immediately, although I make no promise that this is going to be the last the house will hear of it. The minister referred a few moments ago to an interim arrangement which would take care of those persons who have had their benefits drastically curtailed by the reduction which is contemplated, from

Unemployment Insurance Act 51 weeks to 30 weeks. He used a few words in describing these people which brought home to me, even more forcibly than an examination of the bill had done, just how far the thinking of the government and the commission has gone along the lines of a bureaucratic approach to the administration of this act.
The minister said that after all he had to deal with the average. It is not a case any more of those people having a claim on the fund by reason of contributions they have made; no longer a matter of whether or not a worker had built up over the years an investment, let us say, in this fund; no longer a matter of whether his claim was that of a person who can be deemed to be now permanently unemployed by reason of chronological age or whether he is temporarily unemployed because of a shutdown in the plant in which he is generally employed. No; the minister's remark was that the average was 29 weeks, or some such period. Then he went on to quote percentages, and said that those who claim from 1 to 19 weeks were 90-1 per cent of claimants. Since I took these figures down hurriedly perhaps the minister would correct me if I have made an error. Those claiming from 20 to 29 weeks were 6-4 per cent, and those over 30 weeks 3'5 per cent.
He implied that a great many of these people were not what he termed genuinely in the labour market. I am at a loss to know just what the commission might mean by "genuinely in the labour market". If by "genuinely" they mean that a man is physically able to work, anxious to work, and mentally capable, but happens to be over 60 years of age and therefore is not available to the labour market in their interpretation, then I must object most strenuously to that. In my estimation, if a man who has worked to 60 or 65 years of age and who is still strong physically, capable mentally and willing to work, is told by the employer for whom he has worked for many years in steady employment that his services are no longer required by reason of the fact that the laws of the plant in which he is employed state that on a certain date he must retire from this employment-if this man who is able and willing to work makes application at the district office for employment, the employment officer has just as great an obligation to place him in employment as he has to place a 20-year-old man who applies for employment. The need of that man may be just as great, for all that employment officer knows.
There has been some talk about pension plans. I am not a lawyer, but it seems to

me that I recall reading of certain cases where counsel were prohibited by the presiding officer of the court from referring to the fact that people who were engaged in litigation were covered by insurance. In my estimation the same thing applies here. I do not think it is any business of the officer in charge of any divisional employment service whether or not that man who has been laid off from his work by reason of age is covered by a pension. If we are going to admit that kind of thinking, then we are going to place this unemployment insurance on a means test basis. It was not set up in such a way. These people have paid their premiums, many of them for years and years. Many of them have never had occasion to ask for benefits from the fund.
In the same way many of us have paid premiums for years and years for fire insurance on our homes and business premises. We hope we will never have to call on it, but I am sure no one would shout louder than the persons who have drawn up this act if, when the day finally came that they had a fire in their premises, the insurance company were to say to them, "No, you do not really need those premises anyway; therefore we cannot pay your claim despite the fact that you have paid your insurance premiums for many years. You are no longer eligible for benefits from our company; and after all, if our company paid all these claims we would go bankrupt." That is the type of thinking we find in the case of the officers of the commission who drafted this bill and the minister who made this unfortunate remark this evening.
Even more unfortunate than that remark was his follow up, when he referred to his earlier statement on alternative welfare which he had said would be more appropriate. Apparently, Mr. Speaker, it has been a well kept secret in the cabinet that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) intended, at an appropriate time-and no doubt in response to a provocative question-to make the statement which he made yesterday in this house.

speechtext: I am glad to have corroboration from the government benches.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That was the only reason he spoke.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: We were glad to hear that the government had finally decided to take some action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You should have said "hear, hear" three months ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: However, this evening the Minister of Labour has referred to the remarks of the Prime Minister yesterday which were, I understand, elaborated upon today in the meetings which are taking place.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And in the press.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Apparently the alternative welfare which the minister wishes these persons to accept is nothing more nor less than unemployment relief administered by the welfare department of whatever municipality the worker happens to reside in. I draw to the attention of the minister the fact that such relief is also administered on a means test basis. It always has been so administered, and it always will be. It is available only to those persons who are destitute. For that reason it is useless to the man who has been deprived of employment by reason of the fact that he has reached a certain stage in life, namely the stage where his only sin, let us say, Mr. Speaker, is that of having grown older than his employers wish him to be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The colour of his hair has something to do with it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
You mean if he has any hair left. This man has a right to a proper benefit from a fund which he himself has helped to build up. He has a right to insurance. For this government, through these commission offices, to tell that man that the only relief available to him is the relief afforded through the welfare department of his municipality is, in my estimation, an insult to that man.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no one in this house who is not aware of the stigma which is attached to the application for relief afforded only to the destitute. For a man who has been self-sustaining all his life, who has never been laid off from work, who has maintained his family, who now owns his home, who has at length reached retirement age and who is still capable of work, to be told by the commission that there is available to him some assistance in
Unemployment Insurance Act his old age but that he must get it through the local welfare fund is, in my estimation, an insult to that man.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I say to the minister that we are going to fight this clause right straight through until the last vote is called. We have no alternative. I think it is a disgrace and a shame. Because of the lateness of the hour and the fact that I have many more things I should like to say on this bill without interruption, Mr. Speaker, would you please call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not want to interrupt my hon. friend while she was speaking, but in her remarks she referred to workers who were in receipt of pensions and who, she alleged, had been refused unemployment insurance benefits only on account of that fact.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No, no, Mr. Speaker; the minister has misunderstood me. I referred to remarks which were made at the resolution stage of this bill in reference to the fact that, after all, a great many of these people who had retired because of age were in receipt of pensions and accordingly, supposedly, would not require unemployment insurance benefits. I did not say the minister said that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I understood that the hon. member said it was within her knowledge that officials of the unemployment insurance commission had refused benefits because of that fact. I am glad to have her denial.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I did not imply anything of the sort, and I am glad to have the opportunity of setting the matter right.
On motion of Mrs. Fairclough the debate was adjourned.
Tomorrow we shall continue with the debate on the budget.

At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
